claim: African trypanosomes proliferate as bloodstream forms (BSFs) in the mammal.
source: African trypanosomes proliferate as bloodstream forms (BSFs) and procyclic forms in the mammal and tsetse fly midgut, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the life cycle of African trypanosomes.

claim: African trypanosomes proliferate as procyclic forms in the tsetse fly midgut.
source: African trypanosomes proliferate as bloodstream forms (BSFs) and procyclic forms in the mammal and tsetse fly midgut, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the life cycle of African trypanosomes.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics was used to obtain high resolution cell cycle regulated (CCR) transcriptomes of procyclic and slender BSF Trypanosoma brucei without prior cell sorting or synchronisation.
source: Using single-cell transcriptomics on unsynchronised cell populations, we have obtained high resolution cell cycle regulated (CCR) transcriptomes of both procyclic and slender BSF Trypanosoma brucei without prior cell sorting or synchronisation.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodology and results from the abstract.

claim: An efficient freeze–thawing protocol allows single-cell transcriptomic analysis of cryopreserved T. brucei.
source: Additionally, we describe an efficient freeze–thawing protocol that allows single-cell transcriptomic analysis of cryopreserved T. brucei.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a methodological development from the abstract.

claim: Computational reconstruction of the cell cycle using periodic pseudotime inference allowed the dynamic expression patterns of cycling genes to be profiled for both life cycle forms.
source: Computational reconstruction of the cell cycle using periodic pseudotime inference allowed the dynamic expression patterns of cycling genes to be profiled for both life cycle forms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analytical approach and results from the abstract.

claim: A core cycling transcriptome is highly conserved between BSF and PCF forms.
source: Comparative analyses identify a core cycling transcriptome highly conserved between forms, as well as several genes where transcript levels dynamics are form specific.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparative analysis in the abstract.

claim: Several genes have form-specific transcript level dynamics between BSF and PCF forms.
source: Comparative analyses identify a core cycling transcriptome highly conserved between forms, as well as several genes where transcript levels dynamics are form specific.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparative analysis in the abstract.

claim: The majority of genes with periodic cycling transcript and protein levels exhibit a relative delay between peak transcript and protein expression.
source: Comparing transcript expression patterns with protein abundance revealed that the majority of genes with periodic cycling transcript and protein levels exhibit a relative delay between peak transcript and protein expression.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparing transcript and protein data in the abstract.

claim: Metacyclic trypomastigotes emerge from the replicating epimastigote population as arrested G0 forms in the tsetse fly salivary gland.
source: Metacyclic trypomastigotes emerge from the replicating epimastigote population as arrested G0 forms in the tsetse fly salivary gland and express genes required for infection of the mammal, which occurs during their transfer during a bloodmeal (Christiano et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Christiano et al., 2017.

claim: Metacyclic trypomastigotes express genes required for infection of the mammal.
source: Metacyclic trypomastigotes emerge from the replicating epimastigote population as arrested G0 forms in the tsetse fly salivary gland and express genes required for infection of the mammal, which occurs during their transfer during a bloodmeal (Christiano et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Christiano et al., 2017.

claim: Metacyclics re-enter the cell cycle and differentiate into replicative slender bloodstream forms (BSFs).
source: Metacyclics subsequently re-enter the cell cycle and differentiate into replicative slender bloodstream forms (BSFs).
evidence: This is a statement about the life cycle progression of trypanosomes.

claim: Slender BSFs proliferate and increase in parasitaemia before exiting the cell cycle via a quorum sensing mechanism.
source: Slender BSFs proliferate and increase in parasitaemia before exiting the cell cycle via a quorum sensing mechanism (Rojas and Matthews, 2019; Matthews, 2021) and differentiating into G0 arrested stumpy BSFs, which express genes required for differentiation into replicating procyclic forms (PCFs) once in the tsetse fly midgut (Silvester et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rojas and Matthews, 2019 and Matthews, 2021.

claim: Slender BSFs differentiate into G0 arrested stumpy BSFs.
source: Slender BSFs proliferate and increase in parasitaemia before exiting the cell cycle via a quorum sensing mechanism (Rojas and Matthews, 2019; Matthews, 2021) and differentiating into G0 arrested stumpy BSFs, which express genes required for differentiation into replicating procyclic forms (PCFs) once in the tsetse fly midgut (Silvester et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rojas and Matthews, 2019; Matthews, 2021; and Silvester et al., 2017.

claim: Stumpy BSFs express genes required for differentiation into replicating procyclic forms (PCFs) once in the tsetse fly midgut.
source: Slender BSFs proliferate and increase in parasitaemia before exiting the cell cycle via a quorum sensing mechanism (Rojas and Matthews, 2019; Matthews, 2021) and differentiating into G0 arrested stumpy BSFs, which express genes required for differentiation into replicating procyclic forms (PCFs) once in the tsetse fly midgut (Silvester et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Silvester et al., 2017.

claim: The cell cycle of T. brucei broadly follows the typical eukaryotic progression through G1, S, G2, and M phases followed by cytokinesis.
source: The cell cycle of T. brucei broadly follows the typical eukaryotic progression through G1, S, G2, and M phases followed by cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the general cell cycle progression in T. brucei.

claim: Trypanosomes are unusual in that the nuclear and mitochondrial genome is replicated and segregated prior to the nuclear genome in a precisely orchestrated sequence of events.
source: Although, trypanosomes are unusual in that the nuclear and mitochondrial genome is replicated and segregated prior to the nuclear genome in a precisely orchestrated sequence of events.
evidence: This is a statement about the unique features of trypanosome cell cycle.

claim: Many canonical cell cycle regulators remain unidentified, are absent, or have been replaced by trypanosomatid-specific factors in T. brucei.
source: While many canonical regulators remain unidentified, are absent, or have been replaced by trypanosomatid-specific factors.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding cell cycle regulation in T. brucei.

claim: Several cell cycle regulators have been identified in T. brucei including cdc2-related kinases (CRKs).
source: Several regulators have been identified (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022) including cdc2-related kinases (CRKs) (Mottram and Smith, 1995) and 13 cyclins (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022; Lee and Li, 2021), several of which have been linked to regulation of the T. brucei cell cycle phase transitions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: 13 cyclins have been identified in T. brucei.
source: Several regulators have been identified (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022) including cdc2-related kinases (CRKs) (Mottram and Smith, 1995) and 13 cyclins (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022; Lee and Li, 2021), several of which have been linked to regulation of the T. brucei cell cycle phase transitions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several cyclins have been linked to regulation of the T. brucei cell cycle phase transitions.
source: Several regulators have been identified (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022) including cdc2-related kinases (CRKs) (Mottram and Smith, 1995) and 13 cyclins (Hammarton, 2007; Li, 2012; Wheeler et al., 2019; Passos et al., 2022; Lee and Li, 2021), several of which have been linked to regulation of the T. brucei cell cycle phase transitions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Transcriptomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic analysis of semi-synchronised PCF populations have uncovered numerous cell cycle regulated (CCR) genes.
source: Additionally, transcriptomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic analysis of semi-synchronised PCF populations have uncovered numerous cell cycle regulated (CCR) genes for further investigation (Archer et al., 2011; Crozier et al., 2018; Benz and Urbaniak, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Archer et al., 2011; Crozier et al., 2018; Benz and Urbaniak, 2019.

claim: Little overlap has been observed between transcriptomic, proteomic, and phosphoproteomic studies of CCR genes in PCFs.
source: However, little overlap has been observed between these studies (Benz and Urbaniak, 2019), reflecting both the variation between experimental design and differences between transcript and protein regulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Benz and Urbaniak, 2019.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA-seq) allows the transcriptomes of individual cells in a heterogenous, asynchronous population to be captured without the need to first isolate the target cell types.
source: Single-cell transcriptomics (scRNA-seq) allows the transcriptomes of individual cells in a heterogenous, asynchronous population to be captured without the need to first isolate the target cell types by methods such as physical or chemical synchronisation and cell sorting.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of scRNA-seq technology.

claim: Continuous biological processes can be reconstructed in silico using trajectory inference and pseudotime approaches where cells are ordered by their progressive transcriptomic changes.
source: Continuous biological processes, such as cell cycle progression and cellular differentiation, can then be reconstructed in silico using trajectory inference and pseudotime approaches where cells are ordered by their progressive transcriptomic changes (Tritschler et al., 2019; Wolfien et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tritschler et al., 2019 and Wolfien et al., 2021.

claim: scRNA-seq has been used to compare transcriptomes of various T. brucei life cycle stage forms.
source: scRNA-seq has been used effectively to compare transcriptomes of various T. brucei life cycle stage forms, including those extracted from tsetse flies to analyse the development of metacyclics in the salivary gland (Hutchinson et al., 2021; Vigneron et al., 2020; Howick et al., 2022) and to investigate slender to stumpy differentiation of BSFs in vitro (Briggs et al., 2021a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous scRNA-seq studies on T. brucei mainly employed droplet-based methods (Drop-seq and Chromium 10× Genomics).
source: These studies mainly employed droplet-based methods (Drop-seq [Hutchinson et al., 2021] and Chromium 10× Genomics [Vigneron et al., 2020; Briggs et al., 2021a]) to recover higher cell numbers and relied on live, freshly derived parasites to ensure sufficient transcript recovery per cell (Briggs et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous scRNA-seq studies on T. brucei relied on live, freshly derived parasites to ensure sufficient transcript recovery per cell.
source: These studies mainly employed droplet-based methods (Drop-seq [Hutchinson et al., 2021] and Chromium 10× Genomics [Vigneron et al., 2020; Briggs et al., 2021a]) to recover higher cell numbers and relied on live, freshly derived parasites to ensure sufficient transcript recovery per cell (Briggs et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Briggs et al., 2021b.

claim: A previous attempt to use methanol fixed BSFs with Chromium technology yielded low transcript recovery per cell.
source: A previous attempt to use methanol fixed BSFs with Chromium technology yielded low transcript recovery per cell (Briggs et al., 2021b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Briggs et al., 2021b.

claim: Cryopreservation causes limited changes to the transcriptome of BSF and PCF T. brucei.
source: We find cryopreservation causes limited changes to the transcriptome of BSF and PCF T. brucei, highlighting cryopreservation as a valuable method of sample preservation for scRNA-seq analysis of trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Cryopreservation is a valuable method of sample preservation for scRNA-seq analysis of trypanosomes.
source: We find cryopreservation causes limited changes to the transcriptome of BSF and PCF T. brucei, highlighting cryopreservation as a valuable method of sample preservation for scRNA-seq analysis of trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: Periodic pseudotime inference was applied to model the cell cycle progression of both BSF and PCF T. brucei.
source: Periodic pseudotime inference was applied to the resulting data to model the cell cycle progression of both BSF and PCF T. brucei, allowing the genes with CCR transcripts to be identified in each form.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Genes with CCR transcripts were identified in both BSF and PCF forms.
source: Periodic pseudotime inference was applied to the resulting data to model the cell cycle progression of both BSF and PCF T. brucei, allowing the genes with CCR transcripts to be identified in each form.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Comparison with existing high-quality PCF proteomic datasets revealed a relative offset in peak transcript and protein levels for at least 50% of genes exhibiting CCR.
source: Comparison with existing high-quality PCF proteomic datasets (Crozier et al., 2018; Benz and Urbaniak, 2019) further revealed a relative offset in peak transcript and protein levels for at least 50% of genes exhibiting CCR with respect to transcripts and proteins.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparing the study data with published proteomic datasets.

claim: Comparison between BSFs and PCFs identified genes with shared or life cycle stage-specific CCR transcripts.
source: Comparison between BSFs and PCFs identified genes with shared or life cycle stage-specific CCR transcripts, revealing both common and developmentally specific CCR factors, as well as apparent differences in the S–G2 transition between forms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparative analysis.

claim: There are apparent differences in the S–G2 transition between BSF and PCF forms.
source: Comparison between BSFs and PCFs identified genes with shared or life cycle stage-specific CCR transcripts, revealing both common and developmentally specific CCR factors, as well as apparent differences in the S–G2 transition between forms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from comparative analysis.

claim: BSF and PCF cells recovered with high viability after freezing with 10% glycerol, maintaining at least 90% cellular motility after 28 days of cryostorage.
source: Using motility as a measure of parasite viability indicated both BSF and PCF cells recovered with high viability after freezing with 10% glycerol, with each form maintaining at least 90% cellular motility after 28 days of cryostorage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When returned to culture after cryopreservation, parasites showed a delayed return to normal growth rates.
source: When returned to culture, parasites showed a delayed return to normal growth rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating samples should be processed for scRNA-seq immediately after thawing to reflect their transcript status when cryopreserved.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Samples should be processed for scRNA-seq immediately after thawing to reflect their transcript status when cryopreserved.
source: When returned to culture, parasites showed a delayed return to normal growth rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating samples should be processed for scRNA-seq immediately after thawing to reflect their transcript status when cryopreserved.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observation of delayed growth after thawing.

claim: Cryopreservation had little effect on the raw data quality for both BSF and PCF samples.
source: Cryopreservation had little effect on the raw data quality (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1) with the total numbers of unique transcript counts (unique molecular identifiers; UMIs) and features (encoding genes) detected per cell unaffected for either BSF or PCFs (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The total numbers of unique transcript counts (UMIs) and features detected per cell were unaffected by cryopreservation for either BSF or PCFs.
source: Cryopreservation had little effect on the raw data quality (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1) with the total numbers of unique transcript counts (unique molecular identifiers; UMIs) and features (encoding genes) detected per cell unaffected for either BSF or PCFs (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: The percentage of transcripts derived from the mitochondrial kDNA maxicircle genome was unchanged by the freezing and recovery procedures.
source: Additionally, the percentage of transcripts derived from the mitochondrial kDNA maxicircle genome was unchanged by the freezing and recovery procedures (Figure 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of kDNA-derived transcripts was higher in PCF compared to BSF.
source: The percentage of kDNA-derived transcripts was higher in PCF compared to BSF, as expected: only PCFs require complexes III and IV for oxidative phosphorylation (Smith et al., 2017), components for which are encoded on the kDNA maxicircle (Benne, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2017 and Benne, 1985.

claim: Only PCFs require complexes III and IV for oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The percentage of kDNA-derived transcripts was higher in PCF compared to BSF, as expected: only PCFs require complexes III and IV for oxidative phosphorylation (Smith et al., 2017), components for which are encoded on the kDNA maxicircle (Benne, 1985).

claim: Components for complexes III and IV are encoded on the kDNA maxicircle.

claim: Higher average UMIs and features per cell were recovered in PCF compared to BSF, in both fresh and frozen samples.
source: Higher average UMIs and features per cell were also recovered in PCF compared to BSF, in both fresh and frozen samples, although it is unclear if this is a biological phenomenon or if RNA extraction and capture is more efficient from PCFs.

claim: 81.7% and 81.04% of fresh and frozen BSF cells were retained in the data after filtering.
source: After filtering the transcriptomes based on these parameters to remove those of low quality or likely multiplets (Figure 1), 81.7% and 81.04% of fresh and frozen BSFs cells were retained in the data leaving 2767 and 1599 total cells, respectively.

claim: Average transcript counts across cells for each gene were significantly correlated between fresh and frozen samples in both BSF and PCF forms (Pearson's R = 0.977 and 0.985, respectively).

claim: Few genes (BSF: 0.80% of genes captured, PCF: 0.55%) showed greater than twofold difference between fresh and frozen samples.

claim: DE analysis comparing single-cell transcriptomes of fresh and frozen samples revealed 17 genes altered in BSF (14 upregulated in fresh, 3 in frozen).

evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 5.

claim: 522 (28.00%) CCR genes in BSFs had highest expression in G2M.
source: In BSFs, 76 (4.08%) genes had highest expression in early G1, 588 (31.55%) in late G1, 678 (36.37%) in S phase, and 522 (28.00%) in G2M (Supplementary file 5, Figure 3F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 5.

claim: PRI1 localises to the flanking sides of kDNA in BSFs.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy, we found that tagged mNG::PRI1 (N-terminal tag), akin to the observations in PCFs, also localises to the flanking sides of kDNA in BSFs (Figure 3I).
evidence: This statement is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: 27.71% of G1 cells expressed mNG::PRI1, increasing to 78.06% in S phase cells and 67.73% of G2M phase cells.
source: While 27.71% G1 cells were detected as expressing mNG::PRI1, this increased to 78.06% in S phase cells and 67.73% of G2M phase cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: A delay between protein and transcript levels is notable for PRI1, with transcripts peaking in late G1 but protein in S phase.
source: Thus, a delay between protein and transcript levels are also notable for PRI1, with transcripts peaking in late G1 (Figure 3H), but protein in S phase (Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3H, 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tb427_060036900 localises to the nucleus, including in post-mitotic cells where both nuclei contained fluorescent protein.
source: Fluorescence microscopy revealed nuclear localisation, including in post-mitotic cells where both nuclei contained fluorescent protein (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 25.44% of G1 phase BSFs expressed Tb427_060036900::mNG, increasing to 63.04% and 76.72% of S and G2M phase cells, respectively.
source: Flow cytometry revealed 25.44% of G1 phase BSFs expressed Tb427_060036900::mNG, increasing to 63.04% and 76.72% of S and G2M phase cells, respectively (Figure 3J), in keeping with cyclic transcript levels expression increasing in S and G2M phase (Figure 3H).
evidence: This statement is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Tb427_110169500 localises to both the old and newly developing flagellum.
source: N-terminal tagging revealed this protein is expressed in all cycle phases (Figure 3I, J) and localises to both the old and newly developing flagellum (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1013 genes were classed as CCR in both BSF and PCF forms.
source: BSF and PCF CCR transcripts were compared to identify 1013 genes classed as CCR in both forms using a threshold of adjusted p-value <0.01 and FC >1.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 6.

claim: 83.12% (842) of the common CCR genes showed highest transcript levels in the same cell cycle phase between BSF and PCF.
source: 83.12% (842) of the common CCR genes showed highest transcript levels in the same cell cycle phase, and 16.19% (164) peaked in neighbouring phases (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 16.19% (164) of the common CCR genes peaked in neighbouring phases between BSF and PCF.
source: 83.12% (842) of the common CCR genes showed highest transcript levels in the same cell cycle phase, and 16.19% (164) peaked in neighbouring phases (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 260 (25.67%) of the 1013 common CCR genes were shown to have a cell cycle defect in the RIT-seq screen by Marques et al., 2022.
source: Of the 1013 common CCR genes identified here by scRNA-seq analysis, 260 (25.67%) were shown to have a cell cycle defect using the same threshold as Marques et al. (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 6, and comparison with Marques et al., 2022.

claim: CCR orthogroups were conserved across significantly more proteomes (mean of 41.66 out of 44) compared to all orthogroups of the T. brucei Lister427 proteome (mean of 18.44).
source: CCR orthogroups were conserved across significantly (p < 0.0001) more proteomes (mean of 41.66 out of 44), compared all orthogroups of the T. brucei Lister427 proteome (Müller et al., 2018) (mean of 18.44), and a random subset of 1000 orthogroups (mean 18.43) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 540 CCR transcripts were only significant in PCF form.
source: Of the CCR transcripts in PCF, 540 were only significant in this form and showed varied expression across all phases of the cell cycle (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 7.

claim: 851 genes were uniquely DE in BSFs.
source: The 851 uniquely DE genes in BSFs also showed varied expression dynamics over the cell cycle (Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 24 components of the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway were CCR only in BSFs.
source: These metabolic associated genes include 24 components of the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis pathway, including glucose-6-phosphate isomerase (PGI), phosphoglycerate kinase (PGKC), and triosephosphate isomerase (TIM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CYC4 was CCR only in BSFs where transcripts peak in G2/M.
source: In addition, cyclin encoding gene CYC4 was CCR only in BSFs where transcripts peak in G2/M (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CYC9 is significant only in PCFs.
source: In contrast, CYC9 is significant only in PCFs, yet shows only a slight increase in transcript levels as the cell cycle progresses to G2/M (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ZC3H20 displayed cycling transcript levels peaking in G2/M uniquely in the BSF.
source: Master regulator of slender to stumpy differentiation, ZC3H20 (Liu et al., 2020; Cayla et al., 2020), displayed cycling transcript levels peaking in G2/M uniquely in the BSF, along with ZFP1 which is involved in specific repositioning of the kDNA genome during this developmental transition (Hendriks and Matthews, 2005) and also peaks in transcript levels in G2/M phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020; Cayla et al., 2020; and Hendriks and Matthews, 2005.

claim: ZFP1 peaks in transcript levels in G2/M phase uniquely in BSFs.
source: Master regulator of slender to stumpy differentiation, ZC3H20 (Liu et al., 2020; Cayla et al., 2020), displayed cycling transcript levels peaking in G2/M uniquely in the BSF, along with ZFP1 which is involved in specific repositioning of the kDNA genome during this developmental transition (Hendriks and Matthews, 2005) and also peaks in transcript levels in G2/M phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hendriks and Matthews, 2005.

claim: S and G2M BSF cells display less separation in UMAP plots compared to PCFs, indicating less distinction between the transcriptomes of these phases for BSFs.
source: Notably, S and G2M BSF cells display less separation in UMAP plots compared (Figure 3B) to PCFs (Figure 2B), indicating less distinction between the transcriptomes of these phases for BSFs.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 2B.

claim: The switch in gene expression associated with the S–G2 transition is much more discrete or tightly regulated in PCFs than BSFs.
source: This indicates that the switch in gene expression associated with the S–G2 transition is much more discrete or tightly regulated in PCFs than BSFs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the UMAP and pseudotime data.

claim: ATR activity in T. brucei is required for normal S phase progression in both PCFs and BSFs.
source: Interestingly, ATR activity in T. brucei is required for normal S phase progression in both PCFs (Marin et al., 2020) and BSFs (Black et al., 2020), yet the proteins' role in the S–G2 transition differs dramatically between forms.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Marin et al., 2020 and Black et al., 2020.

claim: In BSFs, ATR depletion is lethal and within 24 hr increases the proportions of S and G2M phase parasites, as well as aberrant cells resulting from premature mitosis and cytokinesis events.
source: In BSFs, ATR depletion is lethal and within 24 hr increases the proportions of S and G2M phase parasites, as well as aberrant cells resulting from premature mitosis and cytokinesis events, indicating a putatively similar role to human ATR (Black et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Black et al., 2020.

claim: In PCFs, ATR knockdown has little effect on the cell cycle indicating PCFs mostly undergo the S–G2 transition and complete mitosis and cytokinesis correctly without ATR activity.
source: Yet in PCFs, ATR knockdown has little effect on the cell cycle indicating PCFs mostly undergo the S–G2 transition and complete mitosis and cytokinesis correctly without ATR activity (Marin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Marin et al., 2020.

claim: Even in the presence of persistent DNA damage BSFs will continue to replicate DNA and proliferate.
source: Intriguingly however, even in the presence of persistent DNA damage BSFs will continue to replicate DNA and proliferate (Glover et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Glover et al., 2019.

claim: CYC6 binds CRK3 and is essential for mitosis in both BSF and PCF forms.
source: CYC6 binds CRK3 (Hammarton et al., 2003) and is well characterised as essential for mitosis (Hammarton et al., 2003; Li and Wang, 2003; Hayashi and Akiyoshi, 2018) in both forms, correlating with expression levels detected here at the S–G2M transition.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hammarton et al., 2003; Li and Wang, 2003; and Hayashi and Akiyoshi, 2018.

claim: CYC8 peaks during late G1 in both BSF and PCF forms.
source: CYC8 instead clearly peaks during late G1, despite RNAi depletion leading to a slight increase in G2/M cells in PCFs (Li and Wang, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by data from the study and a citation to Li and Wang, 2003.

claim: Transcripts of both CYC6 and CYC8 are reported to be bound by the RNA-binding protein RBP10.
source: Despite these different patterns, transcripts of both cyclins are reported to be bound by the RNA-binding protein RBP10 (Mugo and Clayton, 2017), highlighting that steady-state RNA levels are likely regulated by multiple factors beyond the individual RBPs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mugo and Clayton, 2017.

claim: RBP10 is not expressed in PCF.
source: Additionally, RBP10 is not expressed in PCF (Wurst et al., 2012; Dejung et al., 2016), and so how matching cyclic expression patterns are regulated in both forms is unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wurst et al., 2012 and Dejung et al., 2016.

claim: In human cells, just 15% of CCR proteins are encoded by genes which also have CCR transcripts.
source: In the human cell cycle, just 15% of CCR proteins are encoded by genes which also have CCR transcripts (Mahdessian et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mahdessian et al., 2021.

claim: A time delay between peak transcript and protein levels was observed in human cells.
source: A time delay between peak transcript and proteins levels was also observed in human cells (Mahdessian et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mahdessian et al., 2021.

claim: Stumpy BSFs upregulate hundreds of transcripts related to PCF biology in preparation for differentiation.
source: A similar observation can be made during T. brucei life cycle progression: stumpy BSFs upregulate hundreds of transcripts related to PCF biology (Briggs et al., 2021a; Kabani et al., 2009; Queiroz et al., 2009; Silvester et al., 2018; Naguleswaran et al., 2018) in preparation for differentiation, but not all upregulated genes are detectable in proteomic analysis of stumpy forms and instead appear after the rapid development of PCFs once the environmental trigger to differentiate has been received (Dejung et al., 2016; Gunasekera et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.
